storyboard.claim: A company's first hire should be an admin, because the CEO's time is being wasted on clerical work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried professional slumped at a desk buried in expense forms and notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues Sister's advice on the first hire.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the clerical drag the first hire removes.

storyboard.claim: Admin work at $15 an hour is far less valuable than strategic thinking worth a thousand an hour.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A spectrum bar with cheap admin work on the left and high-value strategy on the right.
storyboard.onScreenText: Admin work crowds out the big thinking
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the cost of doing admin work yourself.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the value gap visible as a spectrum rather than a number heard once.

storyboard.claim: The company needs strategic thinking from its leader to survive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional talking to the viewer in an office setting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the second expert echoing the advice.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the strategic work that survival depends on.

storyboard.claim: Stop selling raw time for money and sell unique expertise instead.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional pointing outward, rejecting the idea of trading hours for pay.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Quotes the advice to elevate one's own value.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike marks the rejected habit of trading raw hours.

storyboard.claim: The first filter question is whether a task can be dropped entirely.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional thinking over a task list.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts the three-part filter.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists the first of the three questions as on-screen text.

storyboard.claim: If a task is still on the list, ask whether it needs to be done at all.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional weighing a task with a worried look.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Second question of the filter.
storyboard.addedInformation: Restates the filter question in plain words.

storyboard.claim: If the task cannot be delegated, redesign the process so it takes a fraction of the time, and the host admits normal people roll their eyes at this advice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional talking directly to the viewer about changing the process.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Third question of the filter, then the hosts' objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the third option as a process change, not a hire.

storyboard.claim: The CEO-level advice does not fit a solo freelancer with no budget.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried freelancer slumped over a workstation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The host's objection to the executive-level advice.
storyboard.addedInformation: Brings the advice down to a solo worker.

storyboard.claim: Most professionals cannot afford to hire a human assistant.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A discouraged teacher slumped at a classroom desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the objection to teachers and accountants.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts a real budget-limited job on screen.

callout.text: Delegation no longer means hiring a person

storyboard.claim: In the modern era, delegation no longer has to mean hiring a human.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional pondering the old meaning of delegation.
storyboard.onScreenText: Delegation no longer means hiring a person
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the objection by redefining delegation.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the redefinition as on-screen text.

storyboard.claim: Delegation today mostly means using technology to redesign the work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional holding a phone, representing technology doing the work.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines delegation as technology.
storyboard.addedInformation: The phone shows the technology the narration means.

storyboard.claim: A CEO wasted hours a week trading emails with clients to find a meeting time.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried professional thinking with a phone in hand.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the CEO example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the specific waste: back-and-forth emails.

storyboard.claim: Replacing the email back-and-forth with a scheduling app removes the waste.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow from endless emails to a scheduling app.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the CEO example with the fix.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the cause and effect as a flow.

storyboard.claim: The scheduling software sends a link, syncs calendars, creates the video link, and sends reminders.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional pointing at a phone that sends the link.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the scheduling app's steps.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the single action the client takes.

storyboard.claim: The software acts as an admin for pennies a day, and tools like Zapier automate small tasks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional talking while holding a phone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalizes the scheduling example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts a price on the software admin.

storyboard.claim: Nearly any low-level task can now be automated away.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional pointing at the viewer as if handing off the task.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the automation point.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the goal as automating tasks away.

storyboard.claim: The real question is whether a task needs the person's irreplaceable human brain.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A lightbulb over a thinking professional, the brain as the thing to protect.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes the question from paying to thinking.
storyboard.addedInformation: The lightbulb reads as the unique brain-work the narration means.

storyboard.claim: Deciding what deserves your brain is a decision problem, not a scheduling problem.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional thinking through the decision.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the core premise.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts decision-making with scheduling.

storyboard.claim: Not deciding to automate admin means you end up doing the admin yourself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried professional slumped over a stack of notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the host's Exactly.
storyboard.addedInformation: Spells out the consequence of not automating.

storyboard.claim: The person has identified the MIT, blocked the calendar, removed distractions, and automated scheduling.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional holding a target, the most important task.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Recaps the preparation steps.
storyboard.addedInformation: The target stands for the MIT.

storyboard.claim: A biological hurdle remains: how the brain transitions between kinds of work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried professional thinking about the switch.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the next obstacle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the switching problem in plain words.

storyboard.claim: Context switching is the silent killer of focus.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried professional slumped at the office desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the hurdle introduced in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the hurdle a name viewers can keep.

storyboard.claim: A manager is in a heavy one-on-one with a crying employee who needs a performance plan.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sad manager seated with notes in an office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts the manager scenario.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the time and the emotional weight of the meeting.

storyboard.claim: The emotionally draining meeting ends at 1:30 p.m.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A clock showing the meeting end time, and a drained manager.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the manager scenario.
storyboard.addedInformation: The clock shows the exact switch time.

storyboard.claim: The manager jumps straight into a heavy financial spreadsheet at 2 p.m.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager thinking over a spreadsheet at a workstation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the scenario with the switch.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the second, very different task.

storyboard.claim: The manager minimizes the spreadsheet and joins an energetic marketing brainstorm on Zoom.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager talking at a workstation during a video call.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the switch.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the second switch as a fast creative call.

storyboard.claim: By 3 p.m. the manager feels ill, because of attention residue from the switches.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried manager slumped, drained after switching.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the effect of the switches.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the term the book uses for the lingering focus.

storyboard.claim: Switching tasks does not reset the brain instantly; the brain does not simply reboot.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A thinking professional in a quiet library.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the term attention residue's origin.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike rejects the reboot idea the narrator refutes.

storyboard.claim: A large part of the brain stays stuck on the previous task.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried professional thinking with focus stuck in the past.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the reboot rejection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Says what stays behind after a switch.

storyboard.claim: While the manager reads the spreadsheet, half their brain still analyzes the crying employee.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried manager thinking, half attention on the earlier meeting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the residue to the manager example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the split attention in plain words.

storyboard.claim: The manager operates at half capacity, and switching drains mental energy faster than anything else.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sad, drained manager slumped at the desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the cost of the split.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the cost as half capacity.

storyboard.claim: If you must do HR, finance and marketing, how do you survive the switching?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried professional thinking about the workload.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Asks the question the next beats answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the problem as a question for the viewer.

storyboard.claim: Elite performers batch their attention by theming days and refusing hourly jumps between states.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional talking directly to the viewer about the answer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the survival question.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the method as batching.

callout.text: Batch all interviews into one day

storyboard.claim: The podcaster batches all interviews onto one day of the week.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A happy professional talking at a workstation with a studio feel.
storyboard.onScreenText: Batch all interviews into one day
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the first batching example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the schedule concretely.

storyboard.claim: He records interviews back to back and does not switch to writing a blog post in between.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A happy professional talking at a workstation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the podcaster's routine.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the single-mode work.

storyboard.claim: Staying in one mode of work is the principle, scaled to a corporate level by Moskovitz at Asana.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional thinking about staying in one mode.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalizes the podcaster example.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the principle in three words.

storyboard.claim: Asana instituted no-meeting Wednesdays, legally protecting the whole company from interruptions for a full day.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A door shut to keep interruptions out, with a celebrating professional.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from one person to a company-wide policy.
storyboard.addedInformation: The door shows the interruptions being kept out.

storyboard.claim: A full day with no syncs or huddles is dedicated to deep uninterrupted flow, and Sullivan turned this into a system for entrepreneurs.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional thinking in focused calm.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes what the no-meeting day is for.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the goal of the policy.

storyboard.claim: Sullivan tells entrepreneurs to divide their calendar into three distinct types of days.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professional pointing at the viewer, introducing the three types.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces Sullivan's system.
storyboard.addedInformation: Announces the count before the types are named.

callout.text: Keep focus days free of admin

storyboard.claim: Focus days are reserved for the MIT and the highest value revenue work, with no admin allowed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A target standing for the MIT, with the professional pointing at it.
storyboard.onScreenText: Keep focus days free of admin
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the first of the three day types.
storyboard.addedInformation: The target stands for the MIT focus work.
